title: A ? of When with Panda Bear
summary: Pete Kember discusses A ? of When, his collaboration with Panda Bear, Jamaican musical influences and making music with hope for the future. He also reflects on radio and record stores as places to discover music.
transcript:
Pete Kember, Sonic Boom, spoke with Lauren Taylor from Portugal about A Question of When, his second album with Panda Bear. Broadcast on Breaking and Entering, Triple R, 23 July 2026. Edited for length and clarity.

Lauren: Pete Kember was one of the original co-founders of that highly influential UK band Spacemen 3, alongside Jason Pierce. The two famously fell out, and the band dissolved in 1991: they recorded the tracks for their final record together, Recurring, in separate studios, splitting the vinyl down the middle, one side for each artist, and Jason Pierce went on to form Spiritualized. Since Spacemen 3, Pete Kember has continuously pushed the boundaries under different monikers, like Spectrum and E.A.R. and, of course, Sonic Boom. He's also been the secret weapon in the producer's chair for massive records by MGMT and Beach House. And his collaborative partnership with Panda Bear, Noah Lennox of the groundbreaking Animal Collective, goes back to 2011, with Pete co-producing Panda Bear's Tomboy, and also his 2015 release, Panda Bear Meets the Grim Reaper.

The two icons of psychedelic pop are both based in Portugal, Noah for the last two decades and Pete for over a decade now, and they've combined their brilliant musical minds on two albums: 2022's Reset, and now A Question of When, which the band have famously not made available on streaming services. There are no music videos. It's a very intentional decision to keep things, in their words, IRL rather than URL, with the goal of the music creating physical connections between people. They've said the new record deliberately uses sounds and textures they haven't used before, almost a sonic reset after Reset. It's still a total sonic playground, though, packed with everything from Mary Lattimore's harp loops to steel drums to yodelling, and even bits of a mariachi band. And while it sounds incredibly dreamy, the tracks dive into some heavy themes, like online exhaustion and climate anxiety.

I began by asking Pete if they intentionally leaned on these more uplifting sonic textures as an optimistic counterweight to the darker subject matter.

Pete: Yeah, absolutely. And it was the same with Reset. We were dealing with some tricky issues on Reset, and it was something we talked about before starting to work together as Panda Bear and Sonic Boom. I was talking with Noah about how I was always really impressed by Jamaican music from the mid and late 60s. They were dealing with some super tough issues in Jamaica; everything was collapsing and crashing. There's some amazing music that came out of that era, presented in a very positive way, even though they're talking about not being able to get food, and massive inflation, where their money's not worth anything. And they're singing songs about police and thieves; the Junior Murvin track would be a good example. They're talking about tough issues, but in a really beautiful, positive way. So we went into working together with that as one of our touchstones.

Lauren: Would you say the record overall is a hopeful record?

Pete: Yeah. I think you have to be a little realistic when you look out into the world around you and see what's going on. It's very hard not to let that enter your consciousness, but I think you have to be positive, and be looking for ways that things can be different. Most of the problems on this planet are caused by all of us, so it's really all of us who have to act if we want to change that and see things different. If we think someone's going to come along and wave a magic wand, God forbid a politician, then there is no positivity, if you believe that. But if you believe that humans can make good, I think you have to have some positivity.

Lauren: Keeping the vibe musically positive is a conscious choice, but does that joy also happen naturally when you and Noah create music together?

Pete: Yeah. Well, we're trying to amuse and stimulate ourselves, really, and we're sort of indulging each other. I make the music, and I make a lot more of it than we use. I make it to find things that inspire him as much as possible, and what he does always inspires me. It's a very easy working relationship. He's easy to work with. He's very giving. And at the end of the day, if there's anything he doesn't like, I drop it in a flash. It's really important that we both like what we do. We don't really think of it as work and friendship. It's friendship, and we make music within that. We're kind of lucky. I would say I worked hard never to have a real job. But as a musician you're lucky, really, because you are doing what you want to do on your own terms. That might mean you have to eat frozen pizza for a year or two here and there, or in my case a decade or two. But essentially I was happy doing what I wanted to do, so we're very lucky.

Lauren: You've talked about always looking for a new seam of gold to be mined in your working relationship, and about a Goldilocks zone where you can exist nicely. Given how distinct your individual sonic signatures are, what does that zone feel like when you get it just right in the studio?

Pete: I don't know. It was an experiment, really, when we started doing the Reset stuff. I wasn't sure exactly how it could all work out, but it's just been a very natural thing. I guess the rule of thumb is that if we really enjoy it, then possibly other people might, because you never know. Until your record goes out into the world, you have no idea. I've worked with people like MGMT, who had several big hits, and I remember asking them, did you know that was going to be a hit? Did you know 'Kids' was going to be a… They had no idea. In fact, those songs had already been released a year or two earlier, and made zero impact. So you just don't know with these things.

Lauren: The press release says IRL, not URL; more rock and roll, not flick and scroll. The aim is to encourage people to enjoy a real experience in the world and with each other, and you've kept this record off streaming services and everything as offline as possible. That's a bold move today, and you've said you don't think streaming has been good for culture. What's the biggest piece of culture we've lost to convenience, and how does this record claw it back?

Pete: I have this theory, and I doubt I'm the originator of it, but my feeling is, to get creative, the first thing you got to do is get bored. I think once you get bored, that's when your mind starts being creative, and you say, let's form a band, let's write a song. And I think this overly addictive and seductive world that exists in an iPhone, which is being toxified, I mean intentionally, by the platforms who have done it, has really not had a good effect on music and art in general: people getting away from having these real-life interactions.

I think the most magical things in life are things that happen when you least expect. You go out into the world with a good frame of mind and meet people, and magic happens. It's not impossible through a screen, but I think you're less likely to get catfished IRL. That's a phenomenon that only really exists through digital platforms and digital messaging. I just think it's a much better interaction. And some of these things that have been a little overlooked in the streaming era, radio being one of them, are a much more interesting way to consume music.

Lauren: It's interesting you mention radio. Triple R is celebrating 50 years this year. How do you view the role of a radio DJ, or the community station, as an alternative to the modern algorithm? What does radio give the listener that a streaming playlist can't?

Pete: Well, personality, for sure. Once you find a radio station where you like what they do, or particular DJs whose thing you like, it's a magical learning experience. It's a bit like going into a record shop and speaking to the guy who works in there, who has all this knowledge about music but has taste as well, that specific taste. His taste isn't based on what's the most purchased, or the most not purchased. It's not an algorithmic-based thing. I just think it's a much more genuine way to do things, and a nicer interaction, really.

Lauren: I heard the Unfollow Panda Bear and Sonic Boom campaign backfired for you, Pete. You got more followers than ever in one day, is that right?

Pete: Yeah. I don't follow anyone. I never did. I've followed zero since day one, because I felt like if I was going to follow anyone, I had to follow everyone, and I definitely didn't want to do that. And yeah, it was incredibly popular, incredibly successful, that little part of the campaign. It turned out to be part of the campaign, I guess we'll say now, in the rear-view mirror. But I had more followers from that in one day than any other day of doing social media.

Lauren: I wanted to ask about the artwork for the new record as well. Did it originally come from a drawing you did on the back of a napkin? That's amazing. That's so cool. I need to screenshot this moment.

Pete: I can send you the picture, but the artwork on the front sleeve is created by Julian House, based on a sketch I did, I think, is probably the fairest way to say it. His rendition of it is a lot better than mine, I have to say.

Lauren: I don't know, it's pretty good. It's pretty similar to the album cover there.

Pete: I wanted something really propulsive, something that looked like it was in motion, because I think things are seriously in motion. Maybe, at this point, probably unstoppably. I think we're about to see some big changes in society and politics as well. Things have got to the point where it's not a question of if, it's a question of when. That was the inspiration for the album title, and that song, 'A Question of When', really is the centrepiece of the record, what everything else is conversing around.

I like working on different things, with slightly different stylistic things. I don't like to do the same thing the whole time. When I hear something I really like, I usually try and work with the people if I can. That's how I worked with Iceage or Panda Bear. MGMT and Beach House both approached me, but I approach people if I like their music, and say, if you fancy trying some stuff, let's see what happens. We work here informally, out in the countryside in Sintra; I have an informal studio here. It's fun.

I think it's like most places: there's a level of enshittification, which I believe is in the dictionary in Australia. It needed a word for that concept. But this is a place that's been — not being improved by influences.

Lauren: You've said Portugal is seductive. Can you tell me why?

Pete: I think it's really magical because it didn't buy into — Portugal was one of the original third-world countries. The original meaning of a third-world country was a country that didn't take money from America, the first world, or Russia, the second world.

And the fascist dictators they had in Portugal and Spain at that time, Franco and Salazar, were sort of fascism light, I would say, as much as fascism can ever be light. They weren't the worst. They just said, we don't want to be part of it; we don't want the American influence. I'm not anti-American at all, but I think the business model that was fomented in the United States by Bernays and people, and the way that was rolled out onto the world, has not been a good thing. So it's not like that here. Lisbon is such a beautiful city. I still go through areas of Lisbon I've never been through before, and it's just endlessly stunning. It's light on crime. Policing is very hands-off here, which somehow makes the crime lower. It's kind of magical. And of course it's being discovered by other people the whole time; people love to come here, and a lot of digital nomad types come and live here, people who are able to work like myself, whose work is all over the world or online. It's a really great base, a great place to come back to and decompress from the stresses of the modern world, I suppose.

Lauren: Thanks so much for your time, Pete. I really appreciate it, and thanks for all the music over the years as well.

Pete: My pleasure. Thanks for doing the interview.
